title: Job 33:1–18
context: Job 33:1–18 continues Elihu’s speech, now addressed to Job by name. Elihu asks Job to listen, claims sincerity (33:1–3), and grounds his standing in creation: “The Spirit of God has made me, and the breath of the Almighty gives me life” (33:4; compare Genesis 2:7). He says he too is formed from clay, so Job need not fear him (33:6–7). He then summarizes what he has heard Job say: that he is clean and innocent, and that God finds occasions against him, counts him an enemy, puts his feet in the stocks, and marks his paths (33:8–11). Parts of this echo Job’s words closely (compare 13:24, 13:27), while the claim to be wholly without disobedience is stronger than Job’s own wording, since Job also asked God, “Make me know my disobedience and my sin.” (13:23); readers differ on how fairly Elihu summarizes Job. Elihu answers that God is greater than man and does not give account of his matters (33:12–13), and then says that God speaks once or twice, in dreams and visions of the night, to turn a person from wrongdoing and pride and to keep the soul from the pit (33:14–18; compare 4:13; Genesis 20:3; Numbers 12:6). That God warns people in more than one way, to turn them back from destruction, is largely shared ground for both traditions.

verses.text: “However, Job, please hear my speech, and listen to all my words.
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu now addresses Job by name: “However, Job, please hear my speech”. Arminian readers note that Elihu, unlike the three friends, speaks to Job personally and by name, and they see in this a more direct and engaged approach to the suffering man before him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the shift from addressing the friends to addressing Job. They observe that Elihu’s direct appeal sets up his attempt to answer Job’s complaints, and they read the verse as the start of a new phase in the speech rather than as a verdict on its worth.

verses.text: See now, I have opened my mouth. My tongue has spoken in my mouth.
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu says, “See now, I have opened my mouth. My tongue has spoken in my mouth.” Arminian readers note the elaborate and somewhat repetitive opening, which some find solemn and others wordy, and they see Elihu taking care to stress that he is about to speak.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that readers have found this verse either a formal opening or an example of Elihu’s verbosity. They hold such judgments of style loosely, observing that the book records his manner of speech without commenting on it directly.

verses.text: My words will utter the uprightness of my heart. That which my lips know they will speak sincerely.
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu says his words will utter the uprightness of his heart and that his lips will speak sincerely. Arminian readers note that Elihu claims integrity of motive, and they see this as an appeal for Job to trust that he speaks in good faith rather than to win an argument.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that sincerity is a real virtue but does not guarantee correctness. They read the verse as Elihu’s self-description, and they observe that the book invites readers to test his words by what follows, including the LORD’s speeches.

verses.text: The Spirit of God has made me, and the breath of the Almighty gives me life.
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu says, “The Spirit of God has made me, and the breath of the Almighty gives me life.” Arminian readers note the echo of Genesis 2:7, where God “breathed into his nostrils the breath of life”, and they see Elihu grounding his speech in a shared creaturely dependence on God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same echo and the confession that life is God’s gift, shared ground for both traditions. They observe that Elihu uses this truth to claim standing as a fellow creature rather than as a superior, which prepares for his words in 33:6.

verses.text: If you can, answer me. Set your words in order before me, and stand up.
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu invites Job, “If you can, answer me. Set your words in order before me, and stand up.” Arminian readers note that Elihu uses courtroom language, inviting Job to argue his case, and they see this as an offer of a genuine exchange rather than a one-sided lecture.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the language echoes Job’s wish to set his case in order before God (compare 23:4). They observe that Elihu offers himself as a human conversation partner, though readers differ on whether he truly gives Job room to answer.

verses.text: Behold, I am toward God even as you are. I am also formed out of the clay.
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu says, “Behold, I am toward God even as you are. I am also formed out of the clay.” Arminian readers note that Elihu stresses his equality with Job before God, and they hear an echo of Job’s own words that God fashioned him as clay (10:9), named here without harmonizing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Elihu presents himself as a fellow creature, not as a divine voice, and that this tempers any reading of 32:8 as a claim to special status. They read the verse as shared ground on the creaturely condition of every human being.

verses.text: Behold, my terror will not make you afraid, neither will my pressure be heavy on you.
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu says his terror will not make Job afraid, nor will his pressure be heavy on him. Arminian readers note that this answers Job’s plea that God’s terror not make him afraid (9:34; 13:21), and they see Elihu offering the kind of fearless hearing Job asked for.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same allusion to Job’s earlier pleas. They observe that Elihu offers himself as a non-threatening partner, perhaps in partial answer to Job’s longing for an umpire (9:33), while the book leaves open how far Elihu actually fills that role.

verses.text: “Surely you have spoken in my hearing, I have heard the voice of your words, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu says he has heard the voice of Job’s words. Arminian readers note that Elihu bases his response on what Job has actually said, and they see him setting out to answer Job’s own words rather than speculating about hidden sins as the friends did.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Elihu proceeds by quoting and summarizing Job, a method that distinguishes him in part from the three friends. They observe that the fairness of his summary in the following verses is a matter readers assess differently.

verses.text: ‘I am clean, without disobedience. I am innocent, neither is there iniquity in me.
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu quotes Job as saying, “I am clean, without disobedience. I am innocent, neither is there iniquity in me.” Arminian readers note that Job claimed integrity (9:21; 16:17; 27:6), but they observe that he never quite claimed to be sinless, since he asked God to show him his sin (13:23).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that Elihu’s summary is stronger than Job’s own wording, and they hold that readers differ on how fairly it represents him. They see the verse as raising a real issue, the danger of self-justification, while noting the risk of overstatement.

verses.text: Behold, he finds occasions against me. He counts me for his enemy.
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu quotes Job as saying that God finds occasions against him and counts him an enemy. Arminian readers note that this echoes Job’s question to God, “consider me your enemy” (13:24), and they see Elihu accurately capturing Job’s sense of being treated as God’s adversary.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the close echo of 13:24 and observe that this part of Elihu’s summary is fair to Job’s words. They read the verse as Elihu identifying what he sees as the heart of Job’s complaint: that God is acting toward him with hostility.

verses.text: He puts my feet in the stocks. He marks all my paths.’
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu quotes Job: “He puts my feet in the stocks. He marks all my paths.” Arminian readers note that this closely echoes Job’s words, “You also put my feet in the stocks, and mark all my paths.” (13:27), and they see Elihu engaging Job’s actual complaints.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same close echo and the image of a prisoner watched at every step. They observe that Elihu is about to answer this complaint by insisting on God’s greatness, and they read the verse as accurate reporting of Job’s lament.

verses.text: “Behold, I will answer you. In this you are not just, for God is greater than man.
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu answers, “Behold, I will answer you. In this you are not just, for God is greater than man.” Arminian readers note that Elihu’s central point is that Job has spoken wrongly of God, not that Job’s suffering proves past sin, which distinguishes his argument in part from the friends’.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God’s greatness is shared ground for both traditions, and that the LORD’s speeches will also stress it. They observe that readers differ on whether Elihu’s answer anticipates the LORD’s or offers a simpler version of a truth the LORD will present more fully.

verses.text: Why do you strive against him, because he doesn’t give account of any of his matters?
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu asks why Job strives against God, because God does not give account of any of his matters. Arminian readers note that Elihu rebukes Job’s demand for an explanation, and they see a truth both traditions share: God is not obliged to explain his ways to his creatures.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same truth and observe that the LORD later does not explain the prologue to Job. They read the verse as shared ground, while noting that Elihu goes on immediately to say that God does in fact speak to people, in ways they may overlook.

verses.text: For God speaks once, yes twice, though man pays no attention.
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu says, “For God speaks once, yes twice, though man pays no attention.” Arminian readers note that Elihu answers Job’s complaint that God is silent by saying that God speaks in more than one way, and they see an encouragement to listen for God’s voice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the verse affirms God’s initiative in communicating with people, shared ground for both traditions. They observe that the problem Elihu identifies lies with human inattention rather than divine silence, a point that sets up 33:15–18.

verses.text: In a dream, in a vision of the night, when deep sleep falls on men, in slumbering on the bed,
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu says God speaks in a dream, in a vision of the night, “when deep sleep falls on men”. Arminian readers note the close echo of Eliphaz’s vision (4:13), and they compare Genesis 20:3 and Numbers 12:6, named here without harmonizing, as places where God speaks in dreams.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same parallels and treat God’s speaking in dreams as a recognized biblical pattern. They observe that Elihu presents this as one means of divine warning, without claiming that every dream carries such meaning, and they read it as shared ground.

verses.text: then he opens the ears of men, and seals their instruction,
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu says God then opens the ears of men and seals their instruction. Arminian readers note that the image of opening the ear suggests God making a person attentive to a warning, and they see in it God’s gracious initiative to reach people who might not otherwise listen.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that sealing instruction may suggest making it certain or impressing it deeply, though the exact sense of the phrase is discussed. They read the verse as describing God’s effective work in warning a person, shared ground about God’s care.

verses.text: that he may withdraw man from his purpose, and hide pride from man.
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu says God warns people that he may withdraw man from his purpose and hide pride from man. Arminian readers note that the purpose of God’s warning is to turn people from a harmful course, and they emphasize that this invites a response of repentance and humility.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God’s warning aims to remove pride, which they see as a root of sin. They read the verse as shared ground: God acts to turn people from destructive purposes, and the book’s concern with pride will return in the LORD’s speeches.

verses.text: He keeps back his soul from the pit, and his life from perishing by the sword.
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu says God keeps back his soul from the pit and his life from perishing by the sword. Arminian readers note that the purpose of God’s warning is life, not destruction, and they see this as showing God’s merciful intention toward those he warns through dreams and visions.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God’s warning preserves life, and they read the pit as the grave or death. They treat the verse as shared ground about God’s protective purpose, while noting that Elihu now turns from dreams to suffering as another means of God’s speaking.
